title: The Myth of Teaching Children to ‘Read for Pleasure’
author: David Didau
summary: Didau pushes back against the slogans that have accumulated around reading for pleasure: children who read more do better, enjoyment drives attainment, make reading fun and the results will follow. The basic correlation is real, he grants. Children who read widely, often, and with enjoyment do achieve more highly, especially in comprehension and vocabulary. The problem is the direction of causation. Much of the effect appears to run the other way. Stronger readers enjoy reading more because fluency produces pleasure, not the reverse. Pleasure is a lagging indicator of fluency, not its engine. Archive note: the free portion ends before the pay-gated section on the problem with making reading-for-pleasure a curricular aim; the three-part evidence argument above is fully delivered in the open text. He lays down three patterns from recent research. First, reading enjoyment is fragile and is collapsing in ways schools cannot rebrand their way out of. PISA 2022 records the steepest drop in reading enjoyment since international surveys began, and the drop is most pronounced where short-form digital media has crowded out sustained prose. Studies link heavy short-form video use to weaker enjoyment of continuous tasks: repeated exposure to rapid, fragmentary content raises the threshold at which slower cognitive activity feels engaging. In that climate, school strategies that try to make reading fun on TikTok's terms lose the terms they compete on. Second, quality trumps quantity. Stronger readers do not just accumulate pages; they accumulate difficulty, choosing continuous narrative and expository prose with enough syntactic and conceptual stretch to do the cognitive heavy lifting. Children who graze on simple or conversational texts may read a lot without gaining the capacity to handle complex prose. Third, free choice widens gaps unless skill is secure. Skilled readers use autonomy to select challenging books that build vocabulary and inference; weaker readers retreat to comfort texts. Choice without competence becomes a mechanism for stagnation, and autonomy amplifies existing differences rather than equalising them. The closing line is the one worth pinning to a classroom wall: pleasure is a lagging indicator of fluency, and schools cannot shortcut that by sprinkling cushions or running competitions. They can only do the slow work of teaching children to read with accuracy and stamina so that books open rather than resist.
points: The dominant reading curriculum treats books as vehicles for skills instruction, turning reading into work that extracts meaning from text rather than letting readers discover meaning through engagement.

Children whose early reading experiences are structured around comprehension questions, vocabulary flashcards, and test prep learn that reading is something done to them, not something they choose to do.
Pleasure reading builds automaticity, vocabulary, and background knowledge more efficiently than explicit instruction, yet it is sidelined in curricula designed to maximize test performance.
Classrooms that protect time for sustained, choice-driven reading and allow readers to abandon books without penalty produce lifelong readers; classrooms that don't create lifelong book avoiders.
quotes: Although reading for pleasure has become one of education’s unassailable goods, the case for it is not quite as simple as we sometimes pretend. Over the past decade the rhetoric has drifted a long way from the evidence. We repeat slogans as if they were truths: children who read more do better; enjoyment drives attainment; make reading enjoyable and the results will follow. The trouble is that these claims don’t really survive contact with what the best studies actually show.

The leap from correlation to causation is far less certain. Much of the effect appears to flow in the opposite direction: stronger readers tend to enjoy reading more. Fluency produces pleasure rather than pleasure producing fluency. The idea that enjoyment is the engine of achievement has always been more wishful than evidential.

The shift from sustained prose to rapid, novelty-driven browsing appears to make the act of reading feel slow and effortful by comparison. Repeated exposure to fast, fragmentary content raises the threshold at which slower cognitive activities feel engaging. In effect, reading loses its grip because the mind has been conditioned to expect constant stimulation.

In this climate, school strategies that promise to “make reading fun” often ring hollow. They assume reading must compete with TikTok or YouTube on the same terrain. Yet the more reading is framed as entertainment, the more it is judged by entertainment’s standards. When a novel is set against a feed that updates every second, it is hardly surprising that it loses.

What stronger readers accumulate is not just volume but difficulty. They tend to choose continuous narrative and expository prose with enough syntactic and conceptual stretch to deepen comprehension. In other words, they read the kind of texts that do the cognitive heavy lifting.

Children who stick to very simple books, graphic hybrids or short conversational texts may accumulate volume without any substantial gain in their capacity to handle complex prose. The reading diet looks healthy only if you ignore the nutrients.

Skilled readers tend to choose books with enough challenge to build vocabulary and inferential skill. Weaker readers retreat to comfort: texts with predictable syntax, familiar topics and minimal cognitive demand. The result is that autonomy amplifies existing differences rather than equalising them.

Reading for pleasure is good, but not because it magically transforms struggling readers into keen ones. It is good because reading can only become pleasurable once it stops being painfully hard. Pleasure is a lagging indicator of fluency. Schools cannot shortcut this by sprinkling cushions, offering biscuits or running competitions. They can only do the slow work of teaching children to read with accuracy and stamina so that books open rather than resist.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
